lessons.title: Greetings
lessons.intro: How you greet someone in Mexico depends a lot on who they are and how well you know them — getting it right goes a long way before you've said much else.
lessons.didYouKnow: Among friends and family, a single kiss on the cheek is the standard greeting between women, and between a man and a woman — even on a first meeting through a mutual friend. Men greeting other men typically shake hands or, if they're close, share a brief hug.
commonMistakes: Sticking to a stiff handshake with everyone, even close friends of friends, can come across as distant. Mexican greetings tend to be warmer and more physical than many visitors expect.

quiz.question: What's the typical greeting between a man and a woman meeting through a mutual friend?
options: A single kiss on the cheek

quiz.question: "¿Qué onda?" is best used:
options: With your boss on your first day

lessons.title: Restaurant Culture
lessons.intro: Eating out in Mexico runs on a more relaxed clock than many visitors are used to — meals are a social event, not something to rush.
lessons.didYouKnow: Asking for the check is genuinely on you: servers consider it rude to bring the bill before you ask for it, since that can feel like rushing you out. Waiting for it to just appear can mean waiting a very long time.
commonMistakes: Sitting quietly and waiting for the bill to show up on its own — in most sit-down restaurants, it won't, until you flag someone down and ask for it.

quiz.question: In a Mexican restaurant, when will your server usually bring the check?
options: Automatically, right after your last bite
Only when you ask for it
Never — you pay at the entrance

lessons.title: Transportation
lessons.intro: Getting around Mexican cities usually means some mix of metro, buses ("camiones"), and app-based rideshares — each with its own unwritten rules.
lessons.didYouKnow: On Mexico City's metro, the first cars of the train are reserved for women and children only during peak hours, marked with pink signage on the platform.
commonMistakes: Hailing a taxi directly off the street in a big city rather than using a rideshare app or an official taxi stand ("sitio") — it's much harder to verify a random street taxi is legitimate.

quiz.question: What are the pink-marked metro cars in Mexico City reserved for?
options: Women and children during peak hours

quiz.question: What's the safer way to grab a taxi in a big Mexican city?
options: Wave one down anywhere on the street
Use a rideshare app or an official taxi stand
Ask a stranger to call one for you

lessons.title: Shopping
lessons.intro: Shopping in Mexico can mean anything from a fixed-price supermarket to an open-air market ("mercado") where the price is where the conversation starts, not ends.
lessons.didYouKnow: Haggling is expected — and often welcomed — at street markets and with independent vendors, but not at chain stores, malls, or restaurants, where prices are fixed.
commonMistakes: Trying to haggle at a supermarket checkout or a chain retail store — it just won't land, and can come across as odd rather than savvy.

quiz.question: Where is haggling generally welcomed in Mexico?
What does "¿Cuánto cuesta?" mean?
options: Do you have a bigger size?
